---
title: "Quiz: sampling, temperature and the phase transition"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Local field $u_p = J\sum_{q \sim p}s_q + h$; $p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{neighbours}) = 1/(1 + e^{-2u_p/T})$; $J = 1$, $h = 0$ unless stated.

---

**Q1.** Why can a sampler update one pixel without knowing $Z$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the two states that differ only in that pixel.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The update only needs the ratio of the probabilities of two states that differ in one pixel, $e^{-\Delta E/T}$, and $Z$ cancels in a ratio. $\Delta E$ involves only the pixel and its neighbours.
:::

---

**Q2.** A pixel's four neighbours are all $+1$. At $T = 2$, what is the probability that the Gibbs sampler sets it to $-1$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$u_p = 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 - 1/(1 + e^{-4}) = 1/(1 + e^{4}) = 0.018$. Rare, but it happens: at $T = 2$ an aligned region still has a few isolated flipped pixels.
:::

---

**Q3.** In Metropolis, a proposed flip raises the energy. Is it always rejected? Why does that matter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What would the algorithm do if it only went downhill?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: it is accepted with probability $e^{-\Delta E/T}$. Without uphill moves the chain would only descend and stop in the nearest local minimum (that is ICM, next unit); with them it visits states in proportion to their Gibbs probability.
:::

---

**Q4.** What is **detailed balance**, in words?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of traffic between two states after the chain has run for a long time.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In the long run, the chain moves from state $a$ to state $b$ exactly as often as from $b$ to $a$: $\pi_aP_{ab} = \pi_bP_{ba}$. A chain built this way keeps $\boldsymbol\pi$ unchanged, so if it converges at all, it converges to $\boldsymbol\pi$. Metropolis is built so that this holds for the Gibbs distribution.
:::

---

**Q5.** A sampler is started from a noisy image. Why do we throw away the first sweeps, and why are 1000 kept sweeps worth less than 1000 independent samples?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does the chain start, and how much does one sweep change?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The start is not a typical state of the distribution; the first sweeps (the **burn-in**) still remember it. And consecutive states share most pixels: they are strongly **correlated**, so averages over them converge more slowly than over independent samples.
:::

---

**Q6.** Describe a typical state of a large 2D Ising lattice below, at and above $T_c \approx 2.27$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of domain sizes and of $|m|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Below: one sign dominates, with small islands of the other ($|m|$ near 1). At $T_c$: clusters of all sizes, a fractal-looking pattern. Above: fine-grained noise with small clusters ($m \approx 0$).
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is a 1D chain never ordered at $T > 0$, while a 2D lattice is below $T_c$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does it cost to cut a domain in two?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In 1D one disagreeing pair (cost $2J$) splits a chain into two domains, and there are many places to put it: at any $T > 0$ walls appear with a finite density and the signs average out. In 2D a wall around a domain costs energy proportional to its length; below $T_c$ that cost beats the number of ways to draw the wall, and large domains are stable.
:::

---

**Q8.** Simulated annealing is cooled too fast (a quench). What typically goes wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can the lattice still do at very low $T$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Domains form everywhere at once and freeze: at low $T$ only downhill flips are accepted, so walls that would need an uphill flip to move stay forever. The result is a local minimum, not the ground state.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that the Metropolis rule satisfies detailed balance for the Gibbs distribution when $E_b > E_a$ and the proposal is symmetric.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P_{ab} = q\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/T}$ and $P_{ba} = q$ (downhill is always accepted). Then $\pi_aP_{ab} = \frac{e^{-E_a/T}}{Z}q\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/T} = \frac{e^{-E_b/T}}{Z}q = \pi_bP_{ba}$.
:::
